title: The API test layer

story: Nova, our ticket-to-PR agent, is working on a backend ticket: the cloud endpoint that lists projects should sort them by name. It changes one line in the viewset, and now it wants to know whether the endpoint still works. In fcp's backend that question has two answers today, and both are bad for an agent. The unit tests run on Django's own runner and replace the parts that make an endpoint real with mocks. The tests that really call endpoints are the integration tests, and they run on the shared QA environment, where a push waits 20 to 30 minutes for a lock before the first test starts.

So the plan adds a third kind of test that calls the endpoint inside the test process, against a real Postgres. You try a first version with four parallel workers, and every run starts with the same pause: each worker builds its own database by running every one of the cloud's more than 220 migrations, before a single test runs. Nova will run these tests after every edit, dozens of times on one ticket.
hook.question: How can every test worker get a fresh, fully migrated database in seconds, instead of running all the migrations again on every run?

read.h: A third layer: endpoint tests inside the test process
p: fcp's cloud has two kinds of tests today. The unit tests in rhinoCore/tests run with manage.py test, Django's own test runner; they check models and services, and they replace the on-prem client, the object store and the task queue with mocks. The integration tests in rhinoCore/integration-tests call real endpoints over HTTP, but on shared QA, one push at a time. The new layer, a folder called tests_api, sits between the two. A test there sends a request with DRF's APIClient straight into Django inside the same process, as you did in the Django lesson, so the router, the viewset, the serializer, the permission checks and a real Postgres all run, but there is no server, no network and no queue.

The rule for which test goes where is short, so that people and agents can both follow it: a test that calls an endpoint and checks the response goes to tests_api, and a test of one model method or one service stays in rhinoCore/tests. Nobody moves old tests in bulk. The layer runs on pytest with two plugins you met in the pytest lesson: pytest-django, which connects Django to pytest and creates the test database, and pytest-xdist, which shares the tests between several worker processes, here four with -n 4. A test in this layer looks like any DRF test. The one below is from the lab, where a small projects API stands in for fcp's.

notes.text: Every test in this file may use the database. pytest-django refuses database access without this marker.
The request goes through the router, the viewset and the serializer, in this process. The serializer refuses the empty name.

p: Before the first test, pytest-django builds the test database: it creates an empty database named test_ plus the real name, and runs every migration into it. With xdist, each worker is a separate process with its own database (test_app_gw0, test_app_gw1 and so on, where gw0 is the first worker's id), so each worker runs every migration itself. After that, each test runs inside a transaction that is rolled back at the end, so the next test sees the database exactly as the migrations left it. That part is cheap. The expensive part is the migrations, and the next run pays for them again, because pytest-django drops the test databases when the run ends.

In the lab, a small app with 221 migrations needs about 9 seconds for ten tests with -n 4, and the tests themselves take well under one second of that. Now picture fcp: more than 220 migrations that create real tables and indexes, four workers that run them all at the same time on the same machine, and an agent that reruns the tests after every edit.

p: Postgres has a feature that fits this problem exactly. CREATE DATABASE new TEMPLATE old makes the new database a copy of the old one, and Postgres copies the files on disk instead of running anything, which takes a moment even for hundreds of tables. So the layer runs the migrations once, into a template database, and gives each worker its own copy. pytest-django lets you replace the step that builds the database: it is a session fixture called django_db_setup, and a conftest.py that defines a fixture with the same name wins.

Two details make it safe with four workers that start at the same moment. First, an advisory lock: pg_advisory_lock(7007) is a lock with a number we picked, which Postgres holds for us without attaching any meaning to it. The first worker takes it and builds the template; the others wait, then find the template ready and only copy it. Second, Postgres refuses to copy a database while anyone is connected to it, and Django keeps the connection it used for the migrations open, so we close every connection before the copy.

code.file: tests/conftest.py (the lab version; fcp's lives in cloud/rhinoCloud/tests_api/)
code.text:
import hashlib
from pathlib import Path

import pytest
from django.conf import settings
from django.core.management import call_command
from django.db import connection, connections

MIGRATIONS = "".join(sorted(p.name for p in Path("projects/migrations").glob("[0-9]*.py")))
TEMPLATE_DB = "tpl_" + hashlib.sha1(MIGRATIONS.encode()).hexdigest()[:12]  # a new migration means a new name


@pytest.fixture(scope="session")
def django_db_setup(django_db_blocker, worker_id):
    db = settings.DATABASES["default"]
    worker_db = f"test_app_{worker_id}"  # gw0, gw1, ... or "master" without -n
    with django_db_blocker.unblock(), connection._nodb_cursor() as cur:
        cur.execute("SELECT pg_advisory_lock(7007)")  # one worker at a time from here
        cur.execute("SELECT 1 FROM pg_database WHERE datname = %s", [TEMPLATE_DB])
        if cur.fetchone() is None:
            cur.execute(f'CREATE DATABASE "{TEMPLATE_DB}"')
            db["NAME"] = TEMPLATE_DB
            call_command("migrate", verbosity=0)
            connections.close_all()  # a template must have no open connections
        cur.execute(f'DROP DATABASE IF EXISTS "{worker_db}"')
        cur.execute(f'CREATE DATABASE "{worker_db}" TEMPLATE "{TEMPLATE_DB}"')
    db["NAME"] = worker_db
    yield

notes.text: Every migration file name, sorted and joined into one string.
The template's name is a short hash of that string. The next section explains why.
Session scope: this runs once per worker process, not once per test.
worker_id comes from xdist: gw0, gw1 and so on.
A cursor on the server itself, outside any test database, so we can create and drop databases.
Workers queue here. The lock is released when this cursor closes, at the end of the with block.
Only the first worker of the first run with these migrations gets here.
The copy: seconds, whatever the number of migrations.
From now on, Django in this worker opens its own copy.

p: The template is not dropped at the end of the run, so the next run finds it and skips the migrations completely. In the lab the first run with the template takes about 6 seconds and every run after it about 1.5. But a template that is reused forever has a danger: Nova adds a migration, and the tests run against the old schema without the new column. That is why the template's name is a hash of the migration file names. A new migration changes the string, the string changes the name, and the next run looks for a template that does not exist yet, so it builds a fresh one. Nobody has to remember a flag.

fcp's conftest does a little more inside the same block, because the cloud needs it: it creates Django's cache table and loads the same seed fixture that the old unit tests start from, so every copy begins with the same base rows. Anything the template contains should be part of its name, which is the task in this lesson's lab.

deeper.h: Go deeper: the same layer in CI, and a report an agent can read
p: In CI the layer is its own job, API Tests, in the cloud workflow. It starts a throwaway Postgres 17.6 next to the job with the settings that make it fast for tests (fsync, synchronous_commit and full_page_writes off), installs exactly the locked packages of the layer, and runs the tests with four workers. On a fresh CI machine every run is a cold run, so there the win is migrating once instead of once per worker.

Speed alone is not enough for an agent. A 3,000-line pytest log fills its context, so a small pytest plugin writes reports/failures.md after each run: per failing test the test's node ID, the file and line, the first line of the error, the end of the traceback and an exact command that reruns that one test. The tests run in a shuffled but fixed order (pytest-randomly with a fixed seed), and the seed is in the rerun command, so a failure comes back the same way. A second command runs only the tests whose code the change touched, with pytest-testmon from the pytest lesson. testmon cannot see migrations, fixture files or the conftest, because those are read during setup, so a change there runs the whole layer.

lab.title: Migrate once, copy per worker
needs: Docker running (for Postgres 17.6, the version fcp's CI uses)
Port 5432 free. If you already run Postgres there, add -p 5433:5432 to docker run and PGPORT=5433 before each uv run
lab.goal: Measure what migrations cost a parallel test run, then replace pytest-django's database setup with a template that is migrated once and copied for each worker.

guess.q: Your app has 221 migrations and you run ten API tests with pytest -n 4 and pytest-django's default setup. How many times do the migrations run, and what happens on the second run?

options.text: Once in total, because pytest-django shares one test database between the workers.
options.why: Each xdist worker is a separate process with its own database (test_app_gw0, gw1 ...), so each one migrates its own.

options.text: Four times, once per worker, and four times again on the second run.
options.why: Each worker builds its own database, and pytest-django drops them at the end of the run, so the next run starts from zero.
Migrations run once per database, not per test. Each test only gets a transaction that is rolled back.

follow.say: Create a small projects API, the same shape as in the Django lesson, and point it at Postgres.
follow.do:
uv run django-admin startproject mysite . && uv run python manage.py startapp projects
cat >> mysite/settings.py <<'EOF'

import os

INSTALLED_APPS += ["rest_framework", "projects"]
DATABASES = {
    "default": {
        "ENGINE": "django.db.backends.postgresql",
        "NAME": "app",
        "USER": "postgres",
        "PASSWORD": "postgres",
        "HOST": "localhost",
        "PORT": os.environ.get("PGPORT", "5432"),
    }
}
EOF
cat > projects/models.py <<'EOF'
from django.db import models


class Project(models.Model):
    name = models.CharField(max_length=120)
    workgroup = models.CharField(max_length=60)
EOF
cat > projects/views.py <<'EOF'
from rest_framework import serializers, viewsets

from .models import Project


class ProjectSerializer(serializers.ModelSerializer):
    class Meta:
        model = Project
        fields = ["id", "name", "workgroup"]


class ProjectViewSet(viewsets.ModelViewSet):
    serializer_class = ProjectSerializer

    def get_queryset(self):
        return Project.objects.filter(workgroup=self.request.query_params.get("workgroup", ""))
EOF
cat > mysite/urls.py <<'EOF'
from rest_framework.routers import DefaultRouter

from projects.views import ProjectViewSet

router = DefaultRouter()
router.register("api/projects", ProjectViewSet, basename="project")
urlpatterns = router.urls
EOF
uv run python manage.py makemigrations projects

follow.say: Give the app a long history. This script writes 220 more migrations, each creating one small table with an index, which is roughly what a few years of real work look like.
follow.do:
cat > history.py <<'EOF'
"""Write a long migration history, like an app that is a few years old: each migration adds one table."""
import sys
from pathlib import Path

folder = Path("projects/migrations")
done = sorted(p.stem for p in folder.glob("[0-9]*.py"))
for n in range(len(done) + 1, len(done) + 1 + int(sys.argv[1])):
    (folder / f"{n:04d}_step_{n}.py").write_text(f'''from django.db import migrations, models


class Migration(migrations.Migration):
    dependencies = [("projects", "{done[-1]}")]
    operations = [
        migrations.CreateModel(
            name="Step{n}",
            fields=[
                ("id", models.BigAutoField(primary_key=True)),
                ("project", models.ForeignKey("projects.project", on_delete=models.CASCADE)),
                ("note", models.CharField(max_length=200, db_index=True)),
                ("created_at", models.DateTimeField(auto_now_add=True)),
            ],
        ),
    ]
''')
    done.append(f"{n:04d}_step_{n}")
print(f"{len(done)} migrations in {folder}")
EOF
uv run python history.py 220

lab.build: fcp's template also loads a seed fixture, so every copy starts with the same base rows. Do the same here. Create projects/fixtures/seed.json with one project, [{"model": "projects.project", "pk": 1, "fields": {"name": "Demo project", "workgroup": "demo"}}], load it into the template right after migrate with call_command("loaddata", ...), and put the file's content into the hash next to the migration names, so that editing the seed builds a new template. Write tests/test_seed.py with one test that lists the demo workgroup through the API and sees "Demo project". Then change the name in seed.json and run again: a new tpl_ database appears and the test fails, which proves the edit reached the template.
checks: Two runs in a row with the conftest: the second one is several times faster than a run without it.
docker exec academy-pg psql ... lists one tpl_ database per version of your migrations and seed, and test_app_gw0 to gw3.
test_seed.py passes, and the seed row is there in every worker (run with -n 4).
Editing seed.json creates a new tpl_ database on the next run without any flag.
uv run pytest -q without -n also passes: worker_id is then "master" and the copy is test_app_master.

check.q: A teammate asks why the template is called tpl_ plus a hash instead of simply tpl_app. What is the best answer?

options.text: Postgres requires unique random names for template databases.
options.why: Any name works for a template. The hash is our choice, for a reason about migrations.

options.text: So that a new migration gives a new name, and the next run builds a fresh template instead of testing against the old schema.
options.why: The template survives between runs. Without the hash, a new migration would never reach it until someone dropped it by hand.

options.text: So that the four workers do not overwrite each other's template.
options.why: All workers share one template on purpose. Each gets its own copy, test_app_gw0 and so on; the lock keeps them from building it twice.

check.q: Four workers start at the same moment on a fresh Postgres. What does pg_advisory_lock(7007) make sure of?

options.text: That tests in different workers never run at the same time.
options.why: The lock is released before the tests start. The tests run fully in parallel, each in its own database.

options.text: That no other CI job can read the template.
options.why: Each CI job has its own throwaway Postgres. The lock is about the workers inside one run.

options.text: That only the first worker runs the migrations, and the others wait and then copy the finished template.
options.why: Without it, four workers would see no template at the same moment and all try to create it.

check.q: Why is a copy of the template enough for each test to start from a clean database?

options.text: Because pytest-django runs each test inside a transaction and rolls it back, so the copy stays as the template left it.
options.why: Copying gives each worker a clean start once per run; the rollback keeps it clean between tests.

options.text: Because the conftest copies the template again before every test.
options.why: The copy happens once per worker per run. Copying before every test would be slow and is not needed.

options.text: Because API tests never write to the database.
options.why: They write all the time: the lab's tests create projects. The rollback removes those rows after each test.

p: The layer lives in cloud/rhinoCloud/tests_api/ with its own pytest.ini (so it does not inherit the integration tests' markers) and the markers contract and sdk_smoke. Its conftest builds api_tpl_<hash> from the rhinoCore migration names, runs migrate, createcachetable and loaddata of rhinoCore/fixtures/initial_data_prod_aws.json, and copies it per xdist worker. The packages are a uv group api-tests (pytest, pytest-django, pytest-xdist, pytest-randomly, later pytest-testmon). Locally, poe cloud-up-debug exposes Postgres on localhost:5431. The branch had 224 migrations on 12 Oct; the tickets say 228.

In cloud-ci.yml a new job, API Tests, runs pytest tests_api -n 4 on fcp-runner-set with the same Postgres 17.6 service as the test job and uploads reports/ on failure. Root Poe tasks api-test and api-test-affected wrap the layer with seed 1009 and write failures.md and junit.xml. The goals are numbers to watch, not gates: the affected tests in under 30 seconds in the sandbox, the full layer in under 3 minutes on a laptop, the layer plus lint in under 6 minutes in CI. cloud-ci.yml, tests_api/pytest.ini and tests_api/conftest.py become protected paths, so agents cannot change the checks they are judged by.

tickets.why: The decision with the BE guild: which tests go to tests_api, its rules (no eager Celery, no mocks of the client or storage, fake data through the API) and the names the other tickets use.

The API Tests job in cloud-ci.yml with a throwaway Postgres.
failures.md, junit.xml and the fixed random seed, so an agent can read and rerun a failure.

words.plain: tests_api: tests that call an endpoint inside the test process, with a real Postgres but no server or network.
One of the processes pytest -n starts; each has its own id (gw0, gw1 ...) and its own database.
A Postgres database used as the source of CREATE DATABASE ... TEMPLATE, which copies it in seconds.
The pytest-django fixture that builds the test database; a conftest can replace it.
A Postgres lock with a number you choose; here it lets one worker build the template while the others wait.

review.q: Explain to a teammate, in three sentences, why the default setup is slow with -n 4 and what the template changes.
review.a: Each worker builds its own database and runs every migration, and the databases are dropped after the run, so every run pays migrations times workers. The template runs the migrations once and each worker copies it in seconds. Because the template is kept and named after its migrations, later runs skip the migrations until a migration changes.

review.q: A new seed fixture is loaded into fcp's template. What must change in the template's name, and why?
review.a: The fixture's content (or its hash) must be part of the name, like the migration names, so editing it builds a new template instead of reusing old rows.

review.q: Which tests go to tests_api, and which stay in rhinoCore/tests?
review.a: A test that calls an endpoint and checks the response goes to tests_api; a unit test of a model method or a service stays in rhinoCore/tests. No bulk moves.

remember: Run the migrations once into a template named after them, and give every worker a copy: a fresh database in seconds, on every run.
